The objects listed here are still only modules obtained by the parser file. Their later uses determine where they fit in parsing.

```js
let Declaration = require('./declaration')
let tokenizer = require('./tokenize')
let Comment = require('./comment')
let AtRule = require('./at-rule')
```

On line 3, `Declaration` points to `./declaration`; on line 4, `tokenizer` points to `./tokenize`. The former is the module entry point for declaration nodes, and the latter is the adjacent entry point for lexical processing. It is useful to keep both names in the same reading scope, but the two adjacent lines must not be read as a node construction sequence, nor should tokenizer be treated as an alias for Declaration.

The top of the file also contains `Comment`, `AtRule`, `Root`, and `Rule`. Like Declaration, these are node modules obtained by the parser in advance; on this page, they only mark the boundaries of the objects covered in this section. To look up a node's definition, follow its own module name. Do not expand on each node's fields and parent-child relationships in the Declaration entry-point notes.

```text
Top of lib/parser.js
├─ Declaration  → ./declaration
├─ tokenizer    → ./tokenize
├─ Comment      → ./comment
├─ AtRule       → ./at-rule
├─ Root
├─ Rule
└─ SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR
```

This diagram deliberately omits execution order. It records the set of bindings that can be located directly at the top of the file: Declaration is on line 3, tokenizer on line 4, Comment and AtRule on lines 5 and 6 respectively, Root and Rule on lines 7 and 8, and `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` on line 10. To continue reading Declaration, first open `./declaration` and confirm what the node module itself provides; then return to `lib/parser.js` and find the first use of this binding in the file. lib/postcss.d.ts

```text
 └─ AtRule / Comment / Container + Props
             └─ Declarations near the processor interface
```

The early notes called `DocumentProcessor` an "event dispatcher." This came from a quick search: search for the processor name first, then look for callbacks through the declaration entry point. That method could get you to the file, but "visible at the entry point" was casually written up as "organized by the entry point." The same confusion appeared around props. `AtRuleProps`, `CommentProps`, and `ContainerProps` show that the property shapes of the corresponding nodes can be referenced by public interfaces. The two source map imports were also once read too broadly. - If the question is framed in terms of Declaration callback relationships, use the declaration entry point only as a nearby clue; the relevant local notes remain in DOC-06. A full callback explanation is not being added here.

These steps explain why this page is still useful: it can lead readers to neighboring categories of objects in the declarations, and remind them not to treat a type entry point as an event hub. It cannot replace the specific implementation files, much less reconstruct the order of a processing run from the order of the four groups of imports.

This page does not go on to extract the full declaration of every member around `DocumentProcessor`, nor does it add creation, attachment, or modification procedures for each node. So when a search turns up "event output," first read it as an index term near the declaration entry point. To check node interfaces, follow `lib/postcss.d.ts` to the corresponding types; to check Declaration callbacks, switch to DOC-06. # Code-reading notes on Input call relationships

`lib/map-generator.js` started out as just an entry-point note. The old section still contains this straight-line sketch, unchanged:

```text
Input
  -> lib/map-generator.js
  -> source map result
```

That line was useful at the time because it took readers to the baseline source entry point; it also flattened the relationships. The old assessment assumed that, after Input entered, the source map result could be found directly at the end of the file, and that callers shared a single path. A later review found insufficient records within the file to support either assumption, so they should remain as the old account rather than continue to serve as a call graph.

## Read the file itself first

The entry point is fixed at `lib/map-generator.js`. When reading this page, first look at the file's own declarations, then use Input as an index term to return to the middle of the file and find where it first takes part in local processing. There are three distinct objects here: the Input entering the file, the intermediate interactions the file passes directly to dependencies, and the result leaving the file. The old sketch connected them end to end; when tracing them back, record them separately.

This record does not contain specific function names or a complete list of direct dependencies. So "direct dependencies" must be checked against references and call sites in the file itself; names cannot be filled in from other project pages. If a dependency only performs an intermediate transformation, record who uses it and where it returns; do not label it as the final output producer just because it appears at the end of the file. If data is merely passed onward to a local exit, do not interpret it in reverse as a caller of Input either.

## Errors left by the old sketch

Source map-related results are on the exit side. This is a searchable term, not a guarantee about all paths. The old version drew "Input directly obtains a source map result" too straight; after review, only the reading direction of "continue from the entry point to the exits" remains. This still does not establish that every caller goes through the same processing, or that the source map result must be the last step on every path.

Likewise, failure exits and event exits must not be merged. A failure exit means processing did not continue out through the ordinary result path; for an event exit, return to the event emission site and check which part of the local processing triggers it. The available material has no corresponding symbol names, so function or exception types cannot be filled in. When you encounter an error, trace back from the exit points within `lib/map-generator.js`; when you encounter an event, look for the direct caller at the emission site. The entry-point name Input itself cannot replace either check.

```text
Input
  |
  v
lib/map-generator.js
  |                 \
  |                  +-- failure exit
  +-- direct dependencies       +-- event exit
  |
  +-- source map-related results
```

The diagram preserves only the reading direction around this file. It does not represent a complete end-to-end chain, nor does it put failures, events, and source map results into a single chronological sequence. The file contents remain the authority on where intermediate processing takes place; "direct dependencies" in the sketch is only a reminder to return to references and call sites, not a module list that can be copied into an index.

## Boundaries retained after an actual review

The review confirmed that the reading scope should stay around this file and its direct dependencies. It did not confirm that all callers enter through the same Input entry point, or that source map-related results are the same for every kind of input. This page therefore retains only three kinds of local relationships: how Input leads the reader to the file, what the file passes to direct dependencies, and where results, failures, or events leave, respectively.

"Failure exit" and "event exit" here are two directions for tracing back, not two named implementation objects. If specific symbols are later found in the file, they can be added in the corresponding places; until then, writing out function names would make the old record look more certain than it actually is. The same reasoning applies to other entry points for Input: this page does not record their branch differences, so the questions must remain open rather than be answered by a straight-line diagram.

DOC-08 contains old code notes for `CssSyntaxError`. When you encounter that error name, you can read that page's local records alongside this one, but it does not provide the call relationships for `lib/map-generator.js`, nor can it replace tracing back from the failure exit points here. The link between the two pages only indicates that they may be read together; it does not mean one file necessarily calls the other.

## Reading order added later

When revisiting the code, the first step is still to use Input to find `lib/map-generator.js`; the second is to inspect the file's declarations and direct dependencies; the third is to separate intermediate processing from source map-related results; the fourth is to find failure exits and event exits individually. If you only need to confirm the file location, you can stop at the path. To reconstruct call relationships, you must read through the middle of the file rather than judge from just the filename or the two ends of the sketch.

This old page therefore retains two layers: the early straight-line diagram explains how the entry point was located at the time, while the later additions explain why it cannot serve as a complete call graph. # Decision record: rule closing positions and file annotations

The closing positions of compact rules and file annotations were included in the same compatibility review, not because they had been confirmed to share an implementation, but because both can give callers unstable source results. Earlier discussions tracked the issues separately as "rule ending" and "file origin," which made it harder during review to decide whether to look first at the parsing entry point or at the results saved by callers.

There were two approaches at the time.

1. Add a separate internal check for compact rules, taking their closing positions out of the path used for ordinary rules.
2. Keep rules handled by the existing parsing entry point, and retain the position disputes and file annotation disputes side by side as compatibility review material.

Start with the second approach. This is not because the existing position records are considered free of problems, but because there is no evidence supporting a separate set of rules for compact syntax. A separate branch would make "compact" an interface concept, and subsequent calls to Fang Ke could start relying on that classification; the existing records only show that closing positions warrant review, not that the classification itself should be externally visible.

No new storage format is being committed to for file annotations either. Here, "stable" initially means two things: the same file can still be found through the existing discovery entry point; and the relative path and status returned by the tool after discovery should not be lost during the cleanup. Whether annotation fields need to change remains undecided until the actual entry point has been examined.

This round of decisions retains only two constraints: compatibility discussions should focus on the positions and file status callers receive, not on the names of internal helper objects; if later findings show that compact rules can only be fixed with a special branch, first document which visible results that branch changes, then decide whether to accept it.

Early records listed `lib/parser.js` as the sole owning file. That statement was only a starting point for investigation at the time, not a conclusion about module responsibilities. Later reviews can start from that file, but must add the object relationships they find back here; the filename alone cannot establish where positions or file status are stored.

The deferred items are also recorded here: do not establish a public category for compact rules, do not prescribe a field format for file annotations in advance, and do not frame the two topics as work that must be completed in the same change.

# Decision Record on Rule Closure and File Annotations

This record originally grouped the closing position of compact rules with stable file annotations, leaving only the conclusion "do not split out a special branch first." After review, that conclusion needs to be stated more narrowly: what remains grouped is the compatibility issue. This does not mean that both problems are handled by the same piece of code, or that every disagreement about positions must be assigned to the same module.

## The Previous Judgment Still Stands

The initial concern was straightforward. Once compact syntax is treated as a separate category, checks added later can easily shift from "correcting positions" to "providing a set of behaviors for compact rules." There was not enough evidence at the time to justify that divergence, so the choice was to continue investigating from the existing entry point.

This judgment has not been withdrawn. But the old draft presented the "existing entry point" too much like a conclusion: `lib/parser.js` is the starting point for investigation, which does not mean it is responsible for file annotations, rule boundaries, and all call results. The phrase "sole responsible file" in the old draft is marked here as **no longer applicable**. It is retained to explain why the issues were brought together on one page at the time; it should no longer substitute for actually reading the code.

The old draft also had an implicit premise: once the parser was found, the file annotation question could be answered by following the same path. That premise does not hold either. Whether files can be discovered, relative paths can be saved, and tool return statuses can be retained is one aspect of the results; the closing position of a rule is another. The two may be adjacent when reading the code, but they cannot stand in for each other without an actual relationship between the objects.

## Adjacencies Within the File Seen in This Round

What can currently be confirmed is that `lib/parser.js` contains the following declarations:

```js
let Declaration = require('./declaration')
let tokenizer = require('./tokenize')
let Comment = require('./comment')
let AtRule = require('./at-rule')
```

`Root`, `Rule`, and `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` can also be located in the same file. These names are enough to show that this is a junction between reading tokens, forming nodes, and handling adjacent comment objects. On their own, they cannot establish where the closing position is ultimately written, or where file annotations are ultimately saved.

No call graph was built during this reading. All that can be recorded is local adjacency: `tokenizer` is a reading entry point that can be traced; Declaration, Comment, AtRule, Root, and Rule are node objects that can be located in the same file; `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` is an adjacent symbol outside the current scope. The objects appearing together does not mean that they all participate in closing a particular compact rule, or that file state passes through every one of them.

The verification sequence therefore changes to two steps: first, confirm at the parser entry point whether reading compact rules can already distinguish closing characters; then return to the nodes carrying source and the caller's results to confirm whether position and file information are rewritten after leaving the entry point. Do not infer results directly from the name `Rule`, or infer the final offset directly from the name `tokenizer`.

## Two Aspects to Assess

One opinion during the review was that file annotations should be handled independently first: as long as relative paths and tool return statuses are retained, there is no need to wait for the rule position issue to be resolved. Another opinion was that both problems involve source information, and separating them would miss changes to the same data at different stages.

This round did not accept the latter, broader claim. source information can pass through multiple objects, but "the same type of information passes through them" is not enough to demonstrate that all fixes should be submitted together. The decision is to retain two independent aspects to assess:

| Aspect to assess | Provisional decision | What is not being decided in this round |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compact rule closure | Continue tracing visible positions from the parser entry point | Do not create a "compact-rule-specific" interface |
| File annotations | Retain the discovery entry point, relative paths, and tool return statuses as items to check | Do not assume a new field format in advance |

This table replaces the old draft's implication that "the two problems share one fix point." The old draft did not explicitly state that sentence, but its organization made that interpretation easy.

"Independent" in the table does not require the two sides never to meet. It only means that, given the current material, correct positions do not automatically imply correct file annotations, and retained file state does not automatically imply correct rule closure. If a single change to an object is indeed located later, explain which two results that change affects, rather than working backward from the issue names to infer where the implementation belongs.

## The Scope Established by One Review

This was not a complete implementation verification. What was completed was a review within one file: confirming that declarations related to declaration, tokenizer, comment, at-rule, root, and rule all appear in the parser file; and confirming that these object names alone are not enough to identify where stable file annotations are saved. No conclusions were filled in for call chains that had not been read.

This also changes the assessment of the old first proposal. That proposal was to "add dedicated internal checks for compact rules." Its problem was not just that it added branches, but also that it skipped a prerequisite: first, we must know what the existing entry point read, what was saved on the nodes, and what the caller ultimately saw. Without locating these points, dedicated checks would only move the uncertainty to another layer.

The old second proposal was to continue investigating the existing entry point. It is still retained, but its meaning is also limited. It specifies a starting point for reading, not an implementation conclusion; it avoids prematurely exposing a classification, rather than promising that the existing path can already express all the required results. If a local check does prove necessary later, the visible position or saved result it changes should still be stated clearly first.

## Provisional Decision

Continue using `lib/parser.js` as the first place to look, but do not record it as the location responsible for the entire implementation. The closing position of compact rules and stable file annotations remain in the same compatibility document because source-related results for both need to be confirmed in the same review round; their changes, fields, and acceptance checks are not automatically combined.

The local goal for file annotations remains to retain relative paths and tool return statuses after files pass through the existing discovery entry point. This statement adds no fields and does not stipulate that the literal form of paths must remain unchanged forever. On the compact-rule side, we continue to await an assessment of positions that can be tied to the caller's results, without substituting internal helper function names for conclusions.

If later material establishes only one of these items, only that item should be corrected. This applies especially to file annotations: saving relative paths and tool return statuses is the current organizational goal, not an indication that new annotation semantics have already been decided.

## Retained Review Margin Notes

- "First find the layer where the results become visible, then discuss special cases."
- "Being able to navigate from the file entry point does not mean it owns all source state."
- "Compact syntax should not automatically become a public classification."

These margin notes are not implementation instructions. They only constrain how this decision record is brought to a conclusion: accept judgments about behavior only when visible results exist; when there are no results, leave the questions open rather than substituting module names for answers.

## Adjacent Issues Not Split Out

`SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` appears in the declaration list of the same file. It may be related to handling nearby comments, but the current material has not connected it to compact rule closure or file annotations. Leave it outside the decision scope for now; if a later review finds that it changes source results, record the reasons and effects separately.

Another unresolved point is the tool return status in file annotations. The current goal only requires that this status not be lost after discovery; its format, where it is consumed later, and whether it has any relationship to rule boundaries have not yet been specified. This gap should not be filled by the filename of `lib/parser.js`.

# Decision Record: Rule Closure and File Annotation

This material has long been treated as an old entry point within the compatibility window. It was not rewritten from scratch: the early judgments, later-discovered misreadings, one incomplete review, and adjacent issues that have still not been removed all remain in place. What is being added now are decisions that affect caller-visible results, rather than reallocating responsibilities to the parser file.

## The Original Combination

The earliest record listed the closing position of the compact rule alongside file annotation. At the time, there were more names than evidence: the former was called compact-rule closing boundary, and the latter was called stable file annotation. Both were related to source results, so they were placed on the same page; but there was no regression result available for comparison, nor was it clear who was responsible for writing the final position.

Two directions were listed at the time.

- Treat the compact form as an independent category and add a dedicated check for it inside parsing.
- Confirm the relationship between reading, node preservation, and caller-visible results through the existing entry point without defining a new category first.

The original decision chose the latter. The key point of this choice is not "do not change the code," but "do not let the compact form become a new interface before the external behavior has been clarified." If the result can only be corrected through an internal condition later, that condition should still be an implementation detail; callers should not be required to first determine whether a given rule is compact.

The early draft also proposed a very broad file annotation goal: find the file from the discovery entry point, and save the relative path and the status returned by the tool. It did not promise new fields, nor did it interpret "stable" as a permanently unchanged path format. That wording is still useful because it limits the scope of discussion: the focus is whether an identifiable file result is still retained after discovery, rather than renaming all source data.

There was also a practical reason for putting the two objects on one page at the time. The position issue and the file annotation issue had both led readers back to the same parser entry point, and were therefore treated as part of the same round of compatibility cleanup. This archival decision only facilitates traceability; it does not mean they should be brought to closure by the same modification. The old draft did not distinguish the archival relationship from the implementation relationship, and the later misreading began there.

## Limitations of the Early Wording

The early version said, "The compact rule should not automatically become a public category." This judgment remains in force, but it is not a prohibition on implementation branches. What it opposes is requiring users to choose different interface expectations based on the rule's appearance first; if the implementation needs a local condition, that condition may still exist as long as the external result retains the same semantics.

During the same period, "stable file annotation" was written too briefly. That sentence only stated that the result after discovery should be retainable; it did not define where the path is calculated, who creates the status, or how callers consume it. Reading this phrase as a complete file model would go beyond what the material at the time supported.

Therefore, the two items deferred in the early record remain valid: do not presuppose new annotation fields, and do not derive a new caller branch from the appearance-based term "compact." They are not intended to delay the decision, but to prevent unconfirmed internal categories and storage formats from occupying the interface position first.

## Review Addendum from 2023

The first review did not treat the two issues as the same defect. The review's position was: they can be reviewed together, but they cannot be bundled into the same implementation change simply because both carry source information. The dispute over compact rules concerns the closing position; the dispute over file annotations concerns the relative path and tool return status after discovery. The two outcomes need to be confirmed separately.

That review also left a constraint that was repeatedly cited later: do not assert that `lib/parser.js` is the sole owner. The earlier investigation reached this file through issue names and call names, which makes it a suitable starting point for navigation; it is not an assertion about where all source state is generated, copied, or consumed.

This constraint was not included in the body at the time, which later led some people to read "look at the parser first" as "the parser is responsible for everything." The original wording is not being deleted, because it reflects how the search was conducted at the time; it is now clarified as follows: the file entry point is used to begin reading, not to replace the actual relationships between objects.

The review also used "visible results" as a stopping point for the discussion. Here, visibility does not require drawing a complete call graph every time, nor does it require tracing from one file to every node. It only requires being able to explain what the caller actually receives before accepting a judgment about a position; before accepting a judgment about file annotations, it requires being able to explain whether the relative path and tool return status are still retained after discovery.

This constraint allowed the two positions at the time to coexist. One side could continue examining reading operations and node objects near the parser, while the other could continue examining the results after files pass through the discovery entry point; neither side could use the other side's unfinished reading to declare its own position proven.

## In-file review: what can be confirmed

When reviewing `lib/parser.js`, the following declarations can be located:

```js
let Declaration = require('./declaration')
let tokenizer = require('./tokenize')
let Comment = require('./comment')
let AtRule = require('./at-rule')
```

`Root`, `Rule`, and `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` can also be located in the file. These names define a limited scope for reading: tokenizer relates to reading tokens; Declaration, Comment, AtRule, Root, and Rule point to different node objects; `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` points to a local symbol for handling adjacent comments.

The indexed locations are also retained here so that reviewers can return to the same places: Declaration is on line 3, tokenizer is on line 4, Comment is on line 5, and AtRule is on line 6; Root and Rule can each be located in subsequent declarations, and `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` is in the same block of declarations. They are reading anchors, not proof of the complete call order between objects.

Here, "related to" cannot be expanded into a call order. The existing materials do not provide the complete traversal of these objects in a single compact-rule parse, nor do they provide the complete path for the file annotation from discovery to return. Therefore, the review only registers them as adjacencies that can be located again; it does not designate a `require` line as a position write site.

Earlier, one person wanted to infer the finalization boundary directly from where `Rule` appeared, while another wanted to infer where `offset` was generated from the name of `tokenizer`. Neither approach was adopted. Object names can narrow the reading scope, but they cannot replace checking the user-visible result.

Likewise, the fact that `Declaration`, `Comment`, or `AtRule` is imported at the top does not allow us to conclude that they serve the same `source` responsibility across all rule inputs. They show that the `parser` file has broad local adjacency, but they do not show that compact rules necessarily pass through particular objects in sequence. Previously, it was precisely the tendency to misread "visible in the same file" as "owned by the same object" that kept the discussion focused on file ownership.

## Retained Legacy Proposal

> Add a dedicated internal check for compact rules; if ordinary rules already have finalization logic, route the compact syntax to another branch.

This is a legacy proposal and is now marked as **deprecated**. It was not deprecated because "branches are always bad," but because it put classification ahead of the facts. At that time, it had not been established what position the caller actually needed, nor had it been shown that the existing path could not express that position. Creating a branch specifically for compact syntax would cause subsequent users to mistake compactness for a behavioral dimension that needed to be identified.

This section was retained for another reason: it explains why the early pages once focused on internal checks. It was not an approved design, only a candidate proposed to narrow the problem. The later review found insufficient material to support that candidate, so it was not carried forward.

The contrasting legacy proposal two was to continue checking the existing entry points. This proposal must not be idealized either. It only specifies what to check first; it does not guarantee that the existing entry points necessarily contain all the answers. If later evidence shows that a node boundary requires a local check, the implementation can be adjusted without exposing a new classification; whether an adjustment is needed will still be determined by the observable result.

The legacy proposal also contained another unstated assumption: if the finalization position were corrected near the `parser`, the file annotation would stabilize as a byproduct. That assumption is no longer applicable either. Both the rule position and the file result after discovery can carry `source` information, but that is insufficient to prove that they share a save point, much less that one regression result covers the other result surface.

## Record of an Incomplete Experiment

Partway through, one review was called an "experiment," but the scope actually completed was small: checking the locatable declarations in the `parser` file and confirming that the file was simultaneously close to the token and multiple node objects; then separating the file annotation and rule finalization into two verification surfaces. The complete call chain was not obtained in this review, and the unknown portions were not disguised as a passing result.

In the old version, this record could easily be read as saying, "The experiment has verified the parser path." That reading is inaccurate. The experiment verified the direction of the search, not the final behavior. It is enough to reject the approach of "deciding based on the module name first," but not enough to establish any object's ultimate responsibility for writing.

Only one working practice remained after review: first confirm the source result visible to the caller, then trace back to `lib/parser.js` and adjacent objects. This sequence is not a general workflow, but a correction for this particular misreading. Treating source filenames, token names, or node names directly as external behavior once caused the discussion to stall at the wrong level.

This experiment also left a negative finding: no material directly connects `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` to compact-rule closure or file annotation. It can continue to serve as a location reference in the same file, but it cannot be included in the current compatibility decision just because its name contains comment or because it is close to other declarations.

## Boundaries of file annotation

stable file annotation was initially just a brief label. The local objective added later was to retain the relative path and the status returned by the tool after a file passes through the current discovery entry point. This objective describes what is retained, not any unconfirmed field, serialization method, or directory policy.

The decision here is not to extend "stable" to mean any of the following:

- Do not state that all paths are identical in every environment.
- Do not state that the parser file owns the file status.
- Do not state that once the compact-rule position is corrected, file annotation is also complete.
- Do not describe the status returned by the tool as already having a fixed format or a fixed consumption point.

Instead, the current material limits it to a reviewable outcome: after a file is found through the existing discovery entry point, its relative path and the status returned by the tool should still be retainable. If a change affects only the rule position, do not use that to claim that file annotation has been covered; if a change affects only retention after discovery, do not describe it as a compact-rule boundary fix either.

This limitation allows the two topics to remain in the same history while preventing them from being forcibly coupled at the implementation level. They belong to the same compatibility cleanup, but the objects being checked are different. If field names, formats, or more detailed file statuses need to be defined in the future, list the candidates and their compatibility costs separately rather than deriving them from the rule-position decision on this page.

## Correction of earlier ownership claims

**Correction of the earlier judgment:** The old draft made "start reading from the parser" sound like a complete approach to locating the issue. It was later confirmed that this phrase is suitable only as navigation. Any judgment about results must return to the source value visible to the caller Fang Ke, or to an object that explicitly retains the relative path and the status returned by the tool.

After the correction, `lib/parser.js` is still retained as the first entry point for three limited reasons: it is the path specified in the earlier investigation; its declarations expose both the tokenizer and several node objects; and it allows subsequent reviews to re-enter from the same local area. There is no fourth, broader reason.

This also explains why `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` was not included in the current decision. Although it is in the same file, there is no evidence that it changes the closing position of compact rules or the file annotation results. Including every adjacent symbol in the compatibility requirements would only expand the scope and obscure the real questions that still need investigation.

The old draft's claim of a "single owning file" remains part of the historical record and is no longer used as a basis for current verification. It once led readers to skip the node and caller results and treat the filename itself as the conclusion. The current correction does not require denying the value of the parser; it only requires restoring its role as an entry-point file rather than an ownership declaration.

## Disagreements During Review

Two brief comments came up repeatedly during review.

> "First look at which layer makes the result visible."

This comment was adopted as the order of assessment for this page. It requires disputes about position to first focus on caller-visible values Fang Ke, before discussing internal reads and node construction. It does not require tracing the complete call graph for every issue.

> "An entry point that supports navigation does not own all source state."

This comment is used to correct the old draft's claim about file ownership. It does not deny the value of the parser; instead, it prevents a local entry point for reading the code from becoming a conclusion about global responsibility.

Another proposal was not adopted: since both issues involve source, a single unified change should close both at once. That proposal lacked sufficient support. Sharing a word does not mean sharing a storage point; one regression test does not automatically cover another result area. The current decision requires separately documenting the visible position of compact rules and the persisted results of file annotations, then determining whether any changes need to be combined.

Another proposal that was not adopted was to first identify the names of internal helper functions or nodes, then infer the test targets from those names. That reverses the proper order. The regression requirements for CSS-201 already focus on user-visible results rather than internal helper function names; internal names can help with reading the code, but should not become pass criteria.

## Review Entry Point for the Year 2025

CSS-201 brought the compact-rule issue back into review. The card calls for adding a repository regression test and emphasizes asserting user-visible results rather than internal helper function names. One point on the card was still unconfirmed during the recheck stage, and it subsequently moved from to-do to review because the implementation had been completed on an existing branch.

This status change does not mean this page has already reached a conclusion about behavior. It only indicates that the issue can enter review based on the existing implementation, while preserving the fact that one local point was still unconfirmed during review. Rewriting "completed on a branch" directly as "all related source results have been verified" would go beyond the scope actually left by the card.

The regression target on the card is the compact-rule closing boundary. It provides this page with an entry point for verifying position results, not a conclusion about the file annotation format. Therefore, file annotations continue to be handled as an independent result area covering the discovery entry point, relative paths, and tool return status; file details that are not yet available are no longer used to fill gaps in the assessment of rule positions.

When following the previous investigation into `lib/parser.js`, readers can first see the tokenizer and multiple node declarations, then write the discovered visible result back to the card's regression target. This back-and-forth path is narrower than "parser is the only owner" and better matches the existing materials: the file is used for locating, while the card is used to confirm user-visible behavior.

## Current decision

After reviewing the previous approach, verifying the contents of the file, and organizing this review entry, the decision is as follows.

The compact rule will not become a new public classification, nor will "whether it is compact" be a condition that callers need to determine. The parsing entry point and node objects can still serve as starting points for reading and locating the implementation, but the criterion for accepting a correction is the externally visible position result. When parsing the compact rule, `source.end.offset` should be recorded as 3 (the zero-based position of the closing curly brace).

This requirement specifies only the visible ending position of the compact rule. It does not specify which local object in `lib/parser.js` writes this value, does not specify the tokenizer's internal representation, and does not require changing the file annotation to use the same implementation path. Regression tests should assert the user-visible result; the internal helper function name is not the interface defined by this decision.

The file annotation follows another decision: after the file passes through the current discovery entry point, its relative path and the status returned by the tool should be retained. No new field name is introduced here, nor is path stability defined as being literally identical across environments. If stronger file-annotation semantics are needed later, candidates and compatibility costs should be proposed separately, rather than being inferred from this offset requirement.

The current version therefore makes the boundary between the two objects explicit: the ending position is a behavioral requirement of the compact rule; the relative path and the status returned by the tool are the storage targets for the file annotation. Both are tracked in the compatibility window, but validation and changes can be carried out separately.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> discovery entry point
  discovery entry point --> parser recheck
  parser recheck --> ending-position check
  parser recheck --> file-annotation check
  ending-position check --> review
  file-annotation check --> review
  review --> [*]
```

The two checking paths in the diagram are shown in parallel to identify the current decision surface; this does not mean that the parser file has already been confirmed to contain two independent implementation branches. They converge at the review because they are handled within the same compatibility window in this round; which item the review accepts still depends on that item's own visible result.

## Content not expanded by the current-position requirement

The current offset requirement does not answer every source question. It does not specify the shape of the range beyond the closing character, define how other rule forms are handled, or confirm that arbitrary nodes will not change position after leaving the parser. Writing all of these unspecified scopes into it would expand a local position decision into an interface specification unsupported by evidence.

Likewise, the file annotation's storage target does not decide how the file will be consumed later. At present, all we know is that the relative path and tool-return status must be retained after the discovery entry point; there is no material establishing which node, serialization method, or caller ultimately uses these values. This gap should remain rather than being filled in with `Root`, `Rule`, or the parser's filename.

Compact notation does not therefore gain a namespace parallel to ordinary rules. The current requirement specifies a visible position; it does not require the caller to accept "compact rule" as an input category. If a later implementation uses a conditional, the existence of that condition cannot change this externally visible boundary.

## Questions still on the page

1. The review record for CSS-201 still retains "one item unconfirmed." This page does not rewrite that unconfirmed statement as an already-approved blanket conclusion; it needs to be pinned to a specific point in the regression results.
2. Whether `SAFE_COMMENT_NEIGHBOR` is related to the two result surfaces in this work has not yet been established. Do not include it in the fix scope merely because it appears in the parser file.
3. The file annotation's "tool-return status" already has a storage target, but there is currently no material defining its more detailed format or downstream consumption method.
4. The node declaration in the parser file provides neighboring context for reading, but has not yet formed a complete call sequence that could replace the regression results.

These questions have not prevented the current-position requirement from being implemented, because they concern the remaining review, adjacent symbols, file-annotation details, and object paths that have not yet been expanded. Nor should they dilute in reverse the already determined location of the compact rule.

## Archival appendix: two outdated examples

### Example one: routing by rule appearance

An old example once proposed sending all rules without whitespace through a separate path, then handling the closure position in that path. This example no longer applies. Rule appearance is not public-facing semantics that this page allows us to establish; it does not answer what result the caller actually sees, nor does it explain why the ordinary path cannot produce the correct position.

This example is retained because it demonstrates a once-tempting shortcut: label the input first, then let the label determine where the implementation goes. The current decision instead requires fixing the visible position first. Only when a particular implementation condition can actually be shown to be necessary should its local presence be discussed; the condition itself does not become the caller's classification basis.

### Example two: treating the file path as an auxiliary parser value

The old example wrote the relative path as part of the parser output and, on that basis, suggested fixing the storage strategy in that file. This example no longer applies either. The only fact retained now is that, after passing through the discovery entry point, the file needs to preserve the relative path and tool-return status; the storage point and format cannot be inferred from the entry filename.

This example also explains why the current page retains both parser navigation and the file-annotation boundary. The former remains a useful local reading entry point, while the latter remains a result that needs to be verified; the two cannot be bound together by the ownership relationship implied by the old example.

The appendix was not deleted because these two examples have each led to a different misreading: one was treating compactness as an interface classification, and the other was treating the navigation file as the owner of all state. When encountering similar recommendations in later reading, refer back to this page's current decision and the two independent outcome areas.

For non-Root nodes, end.line/end.column still points to the last character belonging to the node, not the next position corresponding to offset. Root's end position is the input EOF. Ordinary CSS must round trip unchanged. The rule a{} has start {offset:0,line:1,column:1} and end {offset:3,line:1,column:3}; .a{} has end {offset:4,line:1,column:4}. Different lengths, nesting, declarations, comments, and line breaks use the same boundary rule; offset cannot be fixed at 3. The old interpretation, "the zero-based position of the closing brace," has been superseded.

# Semicolon Ownership and Parameter Spacing Proposal

For this pass, don't treat the semicolon position and the space after the at-rule parameter as the same formatting issue. The former affects the node range, while the latter is more about preserving the original syntax; if they share one cleanup pass, it will be hard to tell which one consumed the character.

Two candidate approaches for now:

- During parsing, base the range on the actual end of the syntax, leaving preceding whitespace in each raw fragment.
- Let the range follow the scan position to the end, then restore the whitespace on the output side.

The second approach has a smaller change surface, but it makes the meaning of the range depend on the state before output. The first requires revisiting the boundaries provided by the tokenizer and confirming that the construction sites for Declaration and AtRule are not each correcting the boundary independently.

Compare parameter spacing in a separate pass. The goal is not to standardize on one layout, but to confirm that the parameterized at-rule does not spontaneously gain or lose spacing after being processed again.

Start by looking at the entry point for lib/parser.js: this is where tokenizer, Declaration, Comment, AtRule, Root, and Rule are all introduced. Find the first point where the range value is received by a node after leaving the tokenizer. If the two paths do share the same scanning logic, then discuss whether to include them in one change; otherwise, split the commits.

# Semicolon Ownership and Parameter Spacing Proposal

After review, I don't recommend putting the two phenomena into one "whitespace normalization" change. The earlier assumption was that the whitespace around the semicolon and the space after the at-rule parameter were both controlled by the same layer; checking through the entry point for lib/parser.js did not provide enough support for that assumption. At the top of the file, tokenizer, Declaration, Comment, AtRule, Root, and Rule are brought in separately, which at minimum indicates that node creation and lexical boundaries need to be traced separately.

The range branch still has two options, but the comparison criterion is now whether a node's source range can still represent the actual syntax closing point, rather than whether the output string looks tidy. With the "scan position to the end" approach, callers would receive a range that includes leading whitespace; that turns a local formatting choice into an interface change. The other approach fixes the boundary when the end delimiter is recognized, with the whitespace still preserved in the raw syntax. The current preference is the latter, but all node construction points have not yet been checked individually.

Spacing for the at-rule parameter should not borrow the range solution. The comparison here is between retaining the existing spacing and uniformly padding it at output: the former is gentler on old inputs, but requires confirming that the raw fragment is not overwritten during node construction; the latter makes it easier to produce consistent text, but may change formatting already retained by callers. Don't add a global cleanup step for this yet.

The review also surfaced an easy point of confusion: Comment and AtRule are both introduced at the same entry point, but that does not mean parameter spacing should be handled by comment-adjacency logic. Comment boundaries involving the childless at-rule are kept separate in DOC-13; this proposal only handles parameter text and the rule-end boundary.

Proceed with two small sample sets. The first changes only the whitespace before the rule and compares whether the end position moves with the whitespace. The second changes only the spacing after the at-rule parameter and compares the original text after reprocessing. If either set requires changing both the tokenizer and multiple node construction points, stop there; don't disguise it as a low-risk formatting fix.

The rollback criteria are correspondingly narrower: if fixing the end boundary prevents a node from preserving an existing raw fragment, or if parameter spacing can only be stabilized by changing the node range, roll back this split and document the shared path again. Still to confirm: after the end delimiter is recognized, do Declaration and Rule both use the same position data directly?

# Proposal for Semicolon Ownership and Parameter Spacing

This revision keeps the original split rather than trying to address both symptoms with a single whitespace cleanup. Feedback from actual use corrected the v1 assessment: the issue is not "whether whitespace should exist," but which object it ends up in. Whitespace at the rule closure changes how the range is interpreted; spaces after at-rule parameters need to be handled separately as an issue of preserving and outputting the original syntax. Fixing both together would leave callers unable to distinguish range changes from text changes.

The investigation starts at lib/parser.js, but that does not establish where the change belongs. The entry point imports `./tokenize`, `./declaration`, `./comment`, and `./at-rule`, so the review should first look at the end boundary supplied by the tokenizer, then check whether Declaration, Rule, or AtRule applies any additional handling when receiving that boundary. This proposal does not depend on whether Root is involved; no changes to it will be planned until a clear receiving point is found.

## Range branch

The previous proposal considered letting the range follow the scan position, then preserving or restoring whitespace on the output side. We will not pursue that direction further. It exposes a temporary lexical scan position through the node interface, and when the same input is processed again, whether the range changes would depend on whether the raw fragment had been reconstructed.

The proposed constraint is narrower: the terminator closes the rule, while whitespace before the terminator still belongs to the preceding raw fragment and is not preserved by expanding the node range. The requirement is now explicit: when there are spaces before a rule, the rule's own `source.end.offset` must stop at the semicolon position, without counting the preceding whitespace in the range.

This does not require deleting that whitespace or rearranging it on the output side. The implementation check should answer only two questions: what boundary does the tokenizer hand off when it encounters a semicolon, and does anything count the preceding whitespace back into the end after node creation? If the second step includes an adjustment, that adjustment point should remain under review in the range branch, rather than being hidden by a parameter-formatting change.

The minimal comparison for the range branch moves only the whitespace before the rule, leaving all other characters unchanged. Observe the same node endpoint on both the first pass and reprocessing. If the endpoint still shifts with the preceding whitespace, record where it lands first; do not hide the behavior by adding an output rule. If fixing the boundary requires changes to multiple unrelated node-construction sites, return this branch to the investigation stage with no commitment to merge.

## Parameter spacing branch

Spacing after at-rule parameters will still be treated as a raw-text issue. This does not assume that all parameters should have the same spacing, or interpret "stable output" as permission to add spaces uniformly. Compare two candidate approaches: preserving the original spacing found during parsing, or adding spacing within defined limits during stringification. The former requires confirming that construction does not overwrite the fragment; the latter would change existing callers' text-formatting conventions.

Samples for this branch should change only the spacing after parameters, without mixing in rule terminators or adjacent comments. Record the text after one pass, then process it again to confirm that the text does not keep drifting. If the two results differ, first check the raw fragment received by AtRule and the point where the stringifier consumes it; do not go back and change the `source` range to achieve superficial consistency.

Comments next to at-rule with no child nodes are not included in this proposal yet. They may pass through Comment's adjacency logic, which is a different question from whether parameter text is preserved. The related investigation remains in DOC-13. This also avoids misrepresenting a single comment counterexample as a formatting rule for all at-rule.

## Merge and withdrawal

The submission can be split into two small changes: the range branch touches only the end-boundary handoff; the parameter branch touches only where the original spacing is stored or output. Both branches need to keep their results stable on reprocessing when their respective inputs are unchanged, but they do not need to share an implementation.

Withdraw the merge plan for this proposal if any of the following occurs: the range branch must depend on parameter formatting to fix the endpoint; the parameter branch can preserve spaces only by expanding the node range; or the investigation finds that the boundary handed off by the tokenizer already excludes the semicolon and the node layer has no explainable compensation. After withdrawal, retain the existing samples and investigation results, and decide again whether the issue should be handled during scanning, node creation, or output.

One point remains unconfirmed: whether Declaration and Rule receive the end position through exactly the same path. This will determine whether the range branch can be limited to a single change site; results from at-rule cannot substitute for that check.

# Semicolon Ownership and Parameter Spacing Proposal

This revision explicitly supersedes the contrary interpretation in the old record; requirements not revised, the four cumulative compatibility streams, and all unfinished scope remain unchanged. Chat cannot cancel scope; lack of disclosure or a service failure does not mean a fact does not exist.

A rule's own semicolon after its closing brace, with optional intervening whitespace, belongs to that rule: source.end.offset must be after the semicolon, and end.line/end.column points to the semicolon. Leading whitespace before a rule does not change its syntactic start, nor can the adjacent next node be counted as its end. The end of .a{}  ; is {offset:7,line:1,column:7}; the start of   a{} ; is {offset:2,line:1,column:3}, and its end is {offset:7,line:1,column:7}; the end of a{}\n ; (where \n represents one newline) is {offset:6,line:2,column:2}. Output preserves the whitespace and semicolon; two consecutive parse/output cycles are stable. The old interpretation that "offset stops at the semicolon position" has been superseded.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Position Offsets and Childless Rules

The first draft from 2023-03-20 records only two adjacent symptoms that may not share a cause: after calling `positionInside`, the position object appears to be missing fields; when a comment follows a childless at-rule, the order of whitespace and semicolons in the output is hard to reconcile. Don't combine these into one issue yet.

The earlier investigation started at `lib/node.d.ts`. Node is declared next to AtRule, Comment, and Container here, making this a useful place to check names; this alone doesn't establish which object changed. For the position issue, retain the line and column values passed at the call site, along with the full shape of the returned object. Capturing only the two numbers the caller ultimately displays isn't enough.

For the childless-rule issue, first ask: does the rule actually have no child nodes?

```
Repro received
├─ Includes a positionInside call
│  ├─ Full returned object available: record the fields the caller reads
│  └─ Displayed values only: stop, get the call result
└─ Comment follows at-rule
   ├─ Confirmed no child nodes: retain the rule ending, semicolon, and whitespace
   └─ Not confirmed: stop, don't use this page to handle it
```

The working hypothesis at the time was that offset might just be a compatibility field belonging to the old caller, so first check whether line and column look normal. This assessment still has no supporting counterexample and must not be used to remove or change existing compatibility handling. For childless rules, all we know is that the original text needs to be retained; whether the comment belongs before the ending, after it, or near the parameters is still pending a snippet.

The adjacent declarations at the top of the file involve `./at-rule.js`, `./comment.js`, and `./container.js`. If the object names don't match, go back to these declarations to confirm the names, then wait for evidence from the call or output. # Troubleshooting tree for position offsets and childless rules

The 2023-06-29 addendum separates descriptions that were previously mixed together. Position object issues start with the call result; comment issues involving a childless at-rule start with the original character sequence. Both symptoms can occur in the same round, but calling them both compatibility window anomalies is no reason to assume they share an implementation.

## Operational notes alongside the old page

When you receive a position repro, save four things: the line that calls `positionInside`, the position passed in, a full dump of the returned object, and the fields the caller subsequently reads or wraps. If all you have is a display of line and column, mark it as incomplete first; don't treat the display layer as the API result. If the wrapper code changes the object's shape, keep the before and after versions side by side as well.

For a comment repro, save a short piece of rule text without cleaning it up. At a minimum, it must show whether at-rule has no child nodes, whether the rule ends with a semicolon, whether there is whitespace before the comment, and which side of the rule the comment is attached to. A snippet formatted by an editor cannot be used to determine the original spacing.

`lib/node.d.ts` is still the entry point referenced by the old investigation notes. The declarations near the top of the file are:

```ts
import AtRule = require('./at-rule.js')
import { AtRuleProps } from './at-rule.js'
import Comment, { CommentProps } from './comment.js'
import Container from './container.js'
```

These lines are only for matching up the names Node, AtRule, Comment, and Container. They are not evidence for the position algorithm or comment stringification. Once the names are matched up, the next step is still to return to the call site and the original text.

## The split in summer 2023

```
Snippet received
├─ Position call?
│  ├─ Yes: keep the full return value
│  │  ├─ Already different before wrapping: stop at the position result
│  │  └─ Different only after wrapping: inspect reads and renaming
│  └─ No: do not take the position branch
└─ Comment after at-rule?
   ├─ Rule has no child nodes and original text is complete: compare ending characters
   ├─ Unknown whether the rule has no child nodes: stop
   └─ Original text has been formatted: obtain the snippet again
```

## 2024-01-08 review addendum

The review pointed out that the early sequence of "first ask whether the caller only reads line and column" made it easy to accept the old assumption too soon. An old call reading only those two fields can explain why it had not yet exposed a difference; it cannot establish that the returned object has no other position information. This annotation did not remove the first draft, because older integrations may still use that read pattern.

Another annotation concerned comments: seeing a Comment object does not mean Comment should be changed first. Whether the rule has child nodes, whether a semicolon is present, and whether there is whitespace between the comment and the ending must be confirmed from the original sample. Otherwise, moving the comment one position just replaces one unexplained symptom with another.

## One failed attempt

During verification, we first changed the caller's adapter layer. The screenshot we had showed only line and column, so everyone treated the extra fields as content added by the caller. After the adapter changes, we still could not answer what shape the object had before wrapping; this attempt left no usable basis for a fix decision. The sequence in the later addendum is: capture the call result first, then look at what the caller selected; not the other way around.

On the childless at-rule side, we also tried starting with the comment object. That attempt did not retain enough original text to establish the rule ending, semicolon, and whitespace, so it cannot support attribution of the cause. The record is retained as a failed example: if all the material says is "the comment disappeared," do not jump straight to Comment, parameters, or stringification.

## Stop conditions still in use

- No complete returned object: record only the display layer and stop determining where the fields came from.
- Unknown whether the rule has child nodes: stop using the childless-rule branch.
- Original text has been formatted: stop comparing whitespace and semicolons.
- Only a declaration file is available: use it only to navigate names, and do not write an implementation conclusion.

DOC-14 has another set of compatibility check records; its samples are not used here to replace the position or childless-rule snippets.
