# Position Offsets and Childless-Rule Troubleshooting Tree

This page was not originally saved as a complete guide. It started with two short descriptions: the shape of the object returned by a call at a certain position differed from the old impression; a at-rule with no child nodes retained a comment afterward, but the trailing whitespace in the output appeared to have changed position. The two were often raised in the same compatibility review round, so they continued to share this record. A shared page does not mean a shared cause.

## 2023-03-20: Names First, Symptoms Later

The initial evidence was sparse. Investigators traced terms such as `positionInside` and `offset` back to `lib/node.d.ts`, and saw that AtRule, Comment, and Container declarations were still connected near Node. At that point, all that could be confirmed were the object names and the file entry; implementation ownership could not be inferred from the file location.

The position anomaly was initially described as "the result may be missing one value." There was no complete returned object, only the line and column numbers displayed on the caller's page. The old note therefore first asked whether the caller read only line and column; if the UI position was not off, it temporarily treated offset as extra information added by the compatibility layer. This was the working hypothesis at the time, not a final conclusion.

The childless-rule side also had only an oral-style note: the comment after the rule seemed to be attached to the end of the parameter. The original was not saved, and whether the rule truly had no child nodes was not separately verified. The draft only asked that the whitespace between the end of the rule, the semicolon, and the comment be recorded next time.

The original sketch was as follows. It reflects how the initial triage was split, not the decision method adopted later.

```
Compatibility issue
├─ Position object: first ask whether the caller reads only line and column
└─ Comment at the end of the rule: first check whether it looks like the end of a parameter
```

This section is retained because old investigations and old comments may still use phrases such as "missing one value" and "end of parameter." If the same terms appear today, first treat them as original descriptions; do not directly rewrite them as implementation conclusions.

## 2023-04-03: Two Lines from the On-Call Shift

The first on-call addendum did not add any code; it only said, "Do not inspect only the final displayed value" and "Whether a rule has child nodes must be listed separately." These two lines were written beside the draft and were not later merged into the main paragraphs, so for a while the page retained both the old sequence and the new reminders.

Each line addresses one very small omission. On the position side, it is necessary to know whether the returned object changed before wrapping; on the comment side, it is necessary to know whether the sample is a childless at-rule. A comment that appears close to the rule cannot substitute for confirming the node structure. If neither question has an answer, the investigation can go no further than collecting materials.

## 2023-05-17: Failure record from changing the adapter layer first

A review initially changed the caller's adapter layer. At the time, only two displayed coordinates were present, and the rationale for the change was that "the additional position fields might merely be compatibility fields retained by the caller." After the change, no one could reconstruct the pre-wrapper object from the record, or distinguish a change in the interface result from the caller deleting keys. This attempt did not produce a repair conclusion, but its failure had a very specific cause: the observation point was placed at the end of the result.

The approach added later was to capture the call result before wrapping it, then list the fields actually read by the caller separately. When the caller reads only line and column, this fact is still useful: it explains why the old interface did not expose more differences; it is no longer used to prove that the complete object has only those two fields.

The same phase also included an attempt to move Comment first. That sample left only "the comment disappeared," without the original character at the end of the rule, so it could not show whether the relationship changed during parsing, in the AST change, or during stringification. That action remains in the history, but is not the default fix. Without the original text, no one can designate a parameter, semicolon, or piece of whitespace as the starting point.

## 2023-06-29: Local verification at the declaration

The adjacency relationship visible in the file header was later transcribed accurately:

```ts
import AtRule = require('./at-rule.js')
import { AtRuleProps } from './at-rule.js'
import Comment, { CommentProps } from './comment.js'
import Container from './container.js'
```

This code addresses whether the object name mentioned in the discussion matches. It does not address which character changed at which stage, nor does it prove that the position call and the comment for a rule with no children belong to the same path. If the incident snippet contains only a type name, without a call or output, checking here is sufficient; do not continue deriving an implementation story from declaration adjacency.

The troubleshooting order was therefore changed to use two entry points. The position entry retains the passed-in position, the complete returned object, and the differences before and after wrapping; the comment entry retains the original rule text, whether the node exists, the end of the rule, the semicolon, whitespace, and the position adjacent to the comment. If a reproduction contains both types of symptoms, store them as two separate sections; do not combine them into "position and comment are abnormal together."

## 2023-08-14: Debate in review

One sentence appeared repeatedly in the review excerpts: "Seeing the adjacent declaration of AtRule and Comment does not mean you have seen the behavior." This was aimed at an overly quick attribution. Someone saw the object name in `lib/node.d.ts` and directly interpreted the comment at the end of the rule with no children as a Comment object being incorrectly taken over; the other side continued to attribute the position-object problem to the caller.

The review did not settle on a shared patch. Instead, it required the first observation point for each of the two issues to be made explicit. For the position issue, the question is whether the difference appears before or after wrapping; for the comment issue, the questions are whether the original rule has no child nodes and whether the order of the trailing characters is still intact. Both branches allow stopping when the available material is insufficient.

This review also did not remove the old statement that "offset is a field added by the caller." The reason was practical: it records why the adapter layer was changed first at the time, and some older calls really do read only the line and column. The old statement should be read in its historical context, not treated as a description of the current interface.

## 2024-01-08: The old single-track approach was crossed out, but remains on record

For a period of time, the on-call team followed the single track below: first check the line and column read by the caller; if both coordinates are correct, do not investigate offset further. If a Comment is visible, first adjust the Comment's original whitespace; if not, check the at-rule parameter.

> Old single-track approach: when the displayed position is correct, do not investigate the complete object; when a comment is close to a rule, start by examining the comment object.

This section is deprecated. Its problem is not that every local observation is invalid, but that it treats the final display as the first point of change and treats "a Comment is visible" as evidence of object ownership. The old paragraph remains here to help identify traces of how early records were handled; actual troubleshooting must not follow this single track.

The review addendum from the same day defined the stopping conditions more narrowly: without the complete return value, do not determine the source of the position fields; without the unprocessed rule text, do not determine the ownership of semicolons, whitespace, or comments; without the node structure, do not call the sample a childless rule. Here, "stop" means the current material is insufficient, not that the root cause has been found.

## 2024-02-19: Add a correction that points back

The correction on the position side is: older calls taking only two coordinates tells us only how the caller consumes the result, not the return shape of the position interface. If the complete objects already differ before wrapping, stop at the position result and do not continue modifying the adapter layer; only if they match before wrapping and differ after wrapping should you trace back through the code that reads, renames, or deletes keys.

The correction on the comment side is: the presence of a Comment object tells us only that this object was seen in the record, not that it is the starting point of the trailing anomaly. First confirm whether the rule has child nodes, then preserve the original text at the end of the rule. When the rule has child nodes, do not apply this branch even if the comment also appears to sit at the end.

These two corrections point to the troubleshooting tree below, rather than establishing a separate set of authoritative rules. The tree must start with questions that the available fragments can answer; when they cannot be answered, retain the unknowns rather than filling the gaps with variable names, type names, or visually estimated distance.

## 2024-04-11: Reformat the troubleshooting tree

```
Reproduction obtained
├─ First find the positionInside call
│  ├─ Found
│  │  ├─ Is a position passed in?
│  │  │  ├─ Yes: leave it as-is
│  │  │  └─ No: stop at the call site
│  │  ├─ Is the pre-wrapper return object available?
│  │  │  ├─ No: record only that the display is incomplete
│  │  │  └─ Yes: compare it side by side with the post-wrapper object
│  │  └─ Which side contains the difference?
│  │     ├─ Pre-wrapper: continue tracing the position result
│  │     ├─ Post-wrapper: check for reads, renames, or deleted keys
│  │     └─ Unclear: do not choose a fix point
│  └─ Not found
│     └─ Do not use positional terms to explain the comment behavior
└─ Then inspect the comment after at-rule
   ├─ Does the rule have no child nodes?
   │  ├─ Yes: continue
   │  ├─ No: leave this branch
   │  └─ Not confirmed: stop
   ├─ Is the original rule still present?
   │  ├─ Yes: preserve the ending, semicolon, whitespace, and comment
   │  └─ No: retrieve the original text again
   └─ Can the adjacent order be determined?
      ├─ Yes: describe the difference by character position
      └─ No: leave only the unknown items
```

This tree does not connect the two entry points to a shared "fix" node. The position return object and the characters at the end of the rule are separate pieces of evidence. Even if they come from the same test input, record them separately: on the position side, record when the object changes; on the comment side, record which adjacent position differs between the original text and the output.

If the only evidence available is a final screenshot, the position branch can confirm at most what the screenshot shows; if the only evidence available is formatted output, the comment branch can confirm at most that the comment was still present. Neither type of evidence can fill in missing intermediate states. If what you have is a declaration fragment from `lib/node.d.ts`, only verify the object names, then return to the reproduction entry point.

## 2024-07-02: Side note on the old approach

One candidate approach was to normalize all "sparse-field" position reports into the two fields line, column, then have the caller calculate the other position values. This approach was not pursued because it conflated the responsibilities of different wrapper layers and did not address cases where the pre-wrapper object had already changed. It remains in the old side note as a record of why the adapter layer was not expanded directly at the time.

The candidate approach on the childless at-rule side was to move trailing comments uniformly to Comment's expected position. This approach was likewise not pursued. As long as the semicolon and whitespace in the rule text are not preserved, the moved output cannot show whether the original relationship was restored; instead, it overwrites the observed differences.

Both of these old approaches look easy, but both bypass the first observation point. When you see a similar suggestion today, first ask whether it includes the pre-wrapper object or an unprocessed rule; if neither is present, return to the stopping point in the tree.

## 2024-10-26: Meeting excerpts and adjacent questions

Someone also asked in passing during the meeting whether at-rule parameter spacing should be included on this page. No conclusion was reached: the existing material only covers cases where a rule has no child nodes and a comment is near the end of the rule. If the comment falls within the parameter text, or there is another stretch of whitespace after the parameters, the comment branch here cannot be applied based on a similar appearance. This question remains unresolved.

Another unresolved issue concerns external wrappers. If the caller passes only a position number, and the variable name does not indicate whether it comes from `positionInside`, this page cannot infer the original call. The call site or the object before wrapping is needed. This gap has not been filled by type declarations, nor have samples been fabricated just because the compatibility window is nearing its end.

The meeting also retained a very short reminder: position and comment issues can appear side by side in the same reproduction, but the report should describe them as two separate local events. That way, when a new snippet for one side becomes available later, no one will mistakenly think the other side must first be proven to hold as well.

## 2025-03-07: Narrowing the starting points for rechecking

The latest cleanup did not change the old paragraphs; it only made "where to start looking" more explicit. For position issues, return to the call site to obtain the returned object, then compare it before and after wrapping; for comment issues, return to the unprocessed at-rule snippet, then confirm the node structure and ending characters. `lib/node.d.ts` can still serve as a navigation point for declaration names, but it cannot replace either kind of evidence from the actual case.

If all that is available is the name Node, AtRule, Comment or Container, record only the name. If all that is available is the variable name `offset`, its name alone cannot establish that it comes from the position API either. Seeing only a comment object is even less grounds for concluding that it belongs at the end of the parameters. Every judgment must stop at what the available snippet actually supports.

## Current wording to retain toward the end

Write the API check for the position branch as follows: when `positionInside` is called, the return value includes zero-based `offset`, `line` and `column` together. This sentence appears only once, replacing the earlier claim that offset was a field added by the caller. If the actual case shows only line and column, first check whether wrapping has occurred; when the display layer does not show the complete returned object, do not change code near the API on that basis.

The comment branch for childless at-rule is not superseded by the criterion above. First confirm that the rule has no child nodes, then compare the rule's original text, ending, semicolon, whitespace, and comment position together. If any item is missing, retain the unconfirmed status; do not choose the same fix point merely because two phenomena appear in the same input.

If the position objects already differ before wrapping, trace back through the position result; if they are the same before wrapping but change after wrapping, trace back by selecting the caller-side field. For comments, if the rule has child nodes, leave this page's branch; if the rule has no child nodes but the original text has been reformatted, retrieve the original text again. The current guidance addresses the troubleshooting order and the field shape of the position interface; it does not claim that these two types of phenomena have a common root cause.

## Two things not yet split out

The first is at-rule parameter spacing. The existing page does not contain enough snippets to show whether whitespace inside parameters and trailing comments are handled at the same code location, so it cannot be renamed and folded into this page. The second is the recovery method after a position is deleted or wrapped. This page only records how to determine which side the difference appeared on; it does not preserve a call chain sufficient to support a recovery algorithm. The adjacent types at the top of the file are as follows:

```ts

import AtRule, { AtRuleProps } from './at-rule.js'
import Comment, { CommentProps } from './comment.js'
import Container, { ContainerProps } from './container.js'

It allows the investigation to continue through the types for source map, AtRule, Comment, and Container, but the old migration record did not mark any of these types as the execution location for wrapper fallback or raw callback. Previously, after seeing these adjacent types, someone directly attributed the callback anomaly to document-related migration; that judgment has not been deleted, but it is no longer used as the basis for the batch operations.

The old approach was to first take a CSS text sample, inspect the declarations of `document` and `input`, and then change the wrapper call and the arguments passed to the callback at the same time. The advantage was that only one sample needed to be maintained, but the drawback was also straightforward: when the result returned by the wrapper changed, there was no way to tell whether the fallback path had changed or the callback had already processed the sample with a different argument order. The first draft did not record where the second state should be read from, so it treated "the sample runs to completion" as completion of both compatibility tasks.

The old sample entry point is now retained, but the migration record is split into two batches. The first batch migrates the old document wrapper sample to a compatibility sample: without changing the CSS text, first record the calling method that triggers fallback, then record the result the wrapper returns to the caller alongside it. Even if internal helper function names change, they should not replace the result of this step. If the returned content differs from the old sample, stop at the wrapper batch and restore the old calling method; do not carry this change forward into adjustments to the callback.

```text
Old wrapper sample
  -> Keep the original CSS text
  -> Switch to the compatible calling method
  -> Record the user-visible result

Result differs
  -> Restore the old calling method
  -> Keep the sample and failure output
```

The second batch migrates the old callback call to a compatible call record. Here, the wrapper's return value is not reused to draw a conclusion. First use an existing test or example to trigger the callback, and separately record the order of the arguments passed in; then record the state after processing in the same place. ```text
Old callback sample
  -> Trigger the callback
  -> Record the argument order
  -> Record the state after processing

Abnormal state
  -> Restore the old argument order
  -> Keep the triggering sample
```

Do not replace the samples, calling methods, and result criteria all at once across the two batches. When the wrapper's result is inconsistent, restore only the wrapper's old call; when the callback's state is abnormal, restore only the callback's old argument order. The old record rolled back both together, often removing samples that were already reproducible, leaving the next investigation to start guessing from the declaration file again. # Zero-Index Warning and Empty-Member Decision Record

This closeout discusses two names in the same place: `zero-index warning boundary` and `empty comma members`. Both fall within the regression scope of the 2026.09 compatibility window, but the existing material does not show that they are caused by the same processing path. Changing them together would conflate a diagnosis issue with an input-sample issue.

## The disagreement at the time

One approach was to assume first that the two items belonged to the same type of boundary and cover both with a single change. The benefit was a smaller patch surface; the drawback was that the warning location and an empty member in comma-separated content are not the same kind of observation: the former requires confirming the boundary near index zero, while the latter first requires confirming what result remains when an empty member is provided as input.

The other approach was to defer one item until the other had been fully reproduced. This would avoid stating the conclusion too early, but the existing boundary names would have no concrete disposition, and it would be impossible to distinguish a later recurrence of the same regression from two independent phenomena.

## Decision

Keep the two items as parallel compatibility checks, without assuming a common cause and without extrapolating one item's conclusion to the other here. `zero-index warning boundary` starts verification from the warning side; `empty comma members` remains a separate sample issue on the input side. If a shared call chain or the same failure result appears later, make a separate decision on whether to merge them.

The verification entry point for the warning item is `lib/warning.js` in `internal/postcss-core`. This entry point is suitable for first confirming where the index-related warning information is generated and whether the position passed by the caller can still produce a stable result. It does not explain comma-separated members; assigning that input issue directly to the warning file would obscure the samples and results that still need to be completed.

There is another reason to handle them in parallel: index zero is often swallowed by an old "no position" judgment, while an empty member can be masked by normal delimiter handling. Both phenomena need to retain their own failure conditions. Splitting the boundaries first will let subsequent regression records show whether the warning position changed or the way list input is accepted changed.

## Verification checkpoints to retain

The warning item should retain a caller that still reaches the existing entry point and record the actual version, entry point, and current result; do not assume the problem still exists based on its name alone. The empty-member item needs a reproducible input sample before deciding whether it should become a repository test or remain only a compatibility observation. When neither side has sufficient material, do not write "not reproduced" as fixed.

If the two are later confirmed to share the same parsing boundary, update this record with the shared conditions and the reason for the change. Until then, tracking them separately is more reliable than making one broad patch.

# Proposal for Declaration Warnings and Empty Selectors

During the compatibility window, split foreign declaration warning and empty selector and list input into two trial tracks. Both can easily be normalized at the entry point, but they need to answer different questions: the former checks whether the warning surfaces at routine call sites; the latter checks where the shape of an empty input changes.

The proposed approach adds no shared permissive switch and makes no changes to public declarations up front. Keep one minimal sample for each track, recording the original input, the call form used, and the actual result. The foreign declaration sample only observes where the warning is visible; the empty selector or list sample only observes shape differences between input and result.

Use `lib/node.d.ts` as a starting point for reading the types for now. It sits alongside AtRule, Comment, and Container, making it a useful reference if the trial has type implications; this layer must not be treated as the implementation location for warnings or empty-input handling.

There are two options: add only standalone samples, or discuss a preservation strategy after the samples show an actual conflict in existing behavior. The first option is selected. If the samples cannot reliably reproduce a difference, or only repeat ordinary success paths, remove the trial content without introducing new fields or compatibility branches.

Still needed: the actual visible form of the foreign declaration warning; minimal inputs and tool output for empty selector and list input; whether the two samples pass through the same runtime location.
versions.change_summary: Split into two input-boundary trial tracks

versions.body:
# Declaration Warnings and Empty Selector Proposal

This iteration's proposal still does not treat foreign declaration warning and empty selector and list input as a single input special case. They appear in the same compatibility window, which only means that both are worth capturing separately; it does not mean they should share an entry point, type field, or regression fixture. The issue with the former is whether a declaration with a foreign property produces a caller-visible notice in existing calls. The issue with the latter is what shape remains after an empty selector, or an empty member in a list, enters the existing processing path. Binding the two problems into one assertion makes it difficult to determine, when it fails, whether the difference was caused by the object's origin, list construction, or subsequent output.

The initial draft proposed two very narrow trial tracks: it does not commit in advance to the form of the warning, nor does it assume that empty members must be accepted or rejected. Each track first obtains a reusable input and then saves the result actually produced by the tool. The proposal's "preserve" does not require the runtime to add a raw-value field; before existing behavior is confirmed, it only requires that the sample not replace the input before passing it to the entry point, and not fill an empty position with a seemingly normal selector.

This review adds the findings from the declaration-side reading. The file header for `lib/node.d.ts` does place several adjacent objects behind the same reading entry:

```ts
import AtRule = require('./at-rule.js')
import { AtRuleProps } from './at-rule.js'
import Comment, { CommentProps } from './comment.js'
import Container from './container.js'
```

This passage only describes adjacency at the type level. AtRule and its property type are imported separately, and Comment also carries the property type; Container enters the file in another form. This is enough to remind us that if the trial ultimately touches the public shape of node, we cannot check only a single declaration name. It does not indicate where foreign declaration warning is generated, nor does it say whether the parser accepts an empty selector or an empty member in a list. The previous idea of treating this file as the implementation entry point for both problems does not hold; instead, it will be used for a type cross-check after the trial.

## Boundaries Retained by the Proposal

The foreign declaration sample should send a declaration marked as foreign through the normal call path and record only three things: what the object looks like before the call, what the caller receives when the call ends, and, if a warning appears, where it is visible. We cannot assume in advance that the warning is an exception, part of the return value, or some other output; these are all things the sample must determine. If the object is accepted without a visible notice, record "no notice observed"; do not infer from this that no notice exists, and do not fabricate a new warning to satisfy the trial name.

The empty selector and list input samples should start from the original source shape. One sample should contain only an empty selector, and the other only an empty member in a list; do not mix in additional syntax changes. When saving them, keep the source, call form, and the tool's actual output together. If the entry point rejects the input before node construction, the stage at which the rejection occurs is itself the result; only if the entry point continues processing is it necessary to compare the returned node or string. Here, we do not treat "the final output looks normal" as a pass, because the empty member may already have been normalized at an earlier stage.

Neither sample should directly call an unverified internal location for convenience. The goal of the trial is the compatibility surface at the normal entry point, not deciding where the behavior belongs in the runtime implementation. The samples may be run by an existing regression entry point or kept as repeatable local fixtures; the specific host location can be decided after the minimal inputs are obtained. There is currently no evidence supporting the addition of a generic test helper layer, nor any reason to adjust the node declaration file for these two samples.

## Optional Changes

**Add only samples and local assertions.** This is the current priority. The foreign declaration sample should assert only the warning boundary that has already been observed consistently; the empty-input samples should assert only the acceptance, rejection, or output shape that has already been observed consistently. The benefit is that it fixes existing behavior to checkable inputs without prematurely writing origin checks or empty-member semantics into the public interface. The drawback is also clear: if callers truly need to distinguish object origins but the existing entry point exposes no stable signal, the fixture can only record the observed behavior; it cannot solve the caller's selection problem.

**Mark the object's origin at the declaration layer.** This direction was previously considered as a candidate because the name foreign declaration easily suggests a type marker. However, `lib/node.d.ts` currently confirms only the declaration adjacency of AtRule, Comment, and Container; it cannot prove that origin information is suitable for storage in the node type. Adding a field or constraint without a runtime counterpart would give type readers a stronger promise than the actual behavior supports. Unless the sample first confirms that callers truly depend on distinguishable origin information, this option will not proceed.

**Add a preservation strategy for the input shape.** Discuss this direction only if the results for empty selector and list input show that information disappears at an inappropriate stage. It must not be understood as meaning that empty members are always valid: acceptance, rejection, and normalization may all be reasonable results of the existing entry point. The question is whether the actual result conflicts with the call surface that needs to remain compatible. Before obtaining the minimal samples, changing any location in the parser, AST mutation, raw syntax, or stringifier is only guesswork, and may expand a local input issue into more node states.

**Combine the two tracks into one large sample.** Not adopted. The observation target for foreign declaration is the warning boundary, while the observation target for empty selector and list input is the input shape; their only commonality is that both were scheduled into this window. After merging them, a single output change cannot be tied to a unique input condition, and the regression record will lose its purpose.

## Recording Method for the Trial

First retain one unprocessed input for each sample. For foreign declaration, record how the declaration was constructed or obtained; for empty input, record the original source text. Then write down the actual call form used, rather than replacing it with a summary such as "node processing." Finally, attach the tool result: whichever parts actually occurred among a visible return, visible error, or visible warning. Parts that did not occur may be left blank; do not fill in "no impact" just to complete the table.

During review, first check whether the input truly remains in the target shape, then whether the call reaches the expected normal entry point, and only then inspect the result. This order has a practical purpose. If the empty list is cleaned up during sample preparation, the later output comparison is meaningless; if the foreign declaration has already been replaced with an ordinary object before entering the call, the absence of a subsequent warning cannot show that the runtime chose silence. The stopping point here is when the sample loses the target condition, not when the result fails to match a particular expectation.

The declaration side participates in review only when a type change is involved. At that time, recheck `lib/node.d.ts` and its adjacency to AtRule, Comment, and Container to confirm that the trial has not unintentionally expanded the public shape. Conversely, seeing these imports cannot substitute for runtime results. The value of the type entry point is to identify potential coupling, not to draw conclusions about the semantics of warning or empty members.

## Current Trade-offs and Withdrawal

For this round, the tentative decision is to accept only independent samples and local assertions directly connected to those samples. We will not introduce an origin marker just because it is convenient for a sample, fill a list with a placeholder selector, or turn empty-input handling into a uniformly permissive mode. If the samples show that the two tracks happen to pass through the same implementation location, the common parts of the fixtures may be reused after the results are available; the assertions must remain separate.

The withdrawal conditions should also be considered separately. If the foreign declaration sample cannot stably preserve the foreign condition, or if the warning has no recordable boundary under the same call form, remove the proposed warning assertion rather than using a type field to fill the gap. If the empty selector and list input sample loses its empty shape during preparation or before reaching the entry point, first correct the sample representation; if a stable result still cannot be obtained after that correction, do not add a preservation strategy. Any change requiring modifications to public declarations, node construction, or output logic should be proposed separately only after the sample clearly indicates a conflict with the existing surface.

The following items remain unconfirmed: the visible form of foreign declaration warning in normal calls; the minimal input and actual output for empty selector and list input; whether the two samples will reach the same runtime path; and, if the types need to change, which existing uses of AtRule, Comment, and Container will be affected. These remain review questions and are not written as compatibility guarantees.

title: Mapped Endpoints and Container Adoption Troubleshooting Tree

versions.body:
# Mapped Endpoints and Container Adoption Troubleshooting Tree

When "mapped origin endpoint" and "container adoption and JSON raws" come up together, first record the two descriptions separately. Older records grouped them because both investigations led back to `lib/map-generator.js`; that was just a convenient starting point for reading at the time, not enough to establish a shared cause.

```text
Changes in origin or in the text after reprocessing
├─ A corresponding map is available
│  ├─ endpoint is missing
│  │  └─ Save the input, output, and map, then revisit the generation entry point
│  └─ endpoint is visible but the result does not match
│     └─ First specify whether the mismatch is in the source or the interpretation of the position
└─ No corresponding map is available
   └─ Do not infer the endpoint from the output
```

On the container side, first retain the shortest input and the first output. If it has already changed on the first pass, record the raws state first; only keep container adoption as a direction to investigate if the first pass is acceptable and the change appears after reprocessing. Without a second-pass result, do not fill in adoption as the issue.

The old working hypothesis was that the two kinds of reports might converge on the map-generation path. It can only guide where to look first; it cannot replace samples or establish that JSON raws is the cause.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Mapped Endpoints and Container Adoption

This page was originally treated as a very narrow troubleshooting entry point: if a report mentioned "mapped origin endpoint", or someone mentioned container adoption and JSON raws, the first step was to check `lib/map-generator.js`. That entry point is still here, but the old wording could easily lead people to assume that seeing both terms in the same report meant they had already identified the same type of issue.

When actually taking over a report, first write down its original wording. Is it saying that the map is missing, that the origin endpoint is missing, that the source the endpoint points to does not match expectations, or that the text has changed after one or more processing passes. Do not start by summarizing it as "the source map is wrong". That summary collapses a text state with no map, a disagreement over interpretation where an endpoint already exists, and a repeated-processing state with an unknown container source into a label that cannot be investigated further.

The tree below preserves the order of the old entry point. Its purpose is to decide what to retain first and when to stop; it is neither an implementation relationship diagram nor a definitive classification of issue causes.

```text
Start: the report mentions map, origin, endpoint, or text changes after another processing pass
│
├─ A. The report explicitly involves a mapped origin endpoint
│  │
│  ├─ A1. No map was retained with the report
│  │   └─ Stop at "mapping material missing"; retain the output, and do not guess the source endpoint.
│  │
│  ├─ A2. A map is available, but the endpoint cannot be verified in this sample
│  │   └─ Retain the original input, the first output, and the corresponding map;
│  │      then use lib/map-generator.js to review the area around generation.
│  │
│  └─ A3. The endpoint is visible, but the report still says the result is wrong
│      └─ Split this into "source object mismatch" and "position interpretation mismatch";
│         do not route it to the container branch.
│
└─ B. The report involves container adoption and JSON raws
   │
   ├─ B1. There is already a difference before and after the first processing pass
   │   └─ Retain the first input and output, and first record where raws changed.
   │
   ├─ B2. The first pass is acceptable, and differences appear only after another processing pass
   │   └─ Retain the first and second outputs, and add the source of the objects used in the second round.
   │
   └─ B3. There is no second result, or the container source was not retained
       └─ Retain it as an incomplete sample; do not record adoption as a confirmed cause.
```

## First Identify What the Report Is Saying

mapped origin endpoint is not a broad phenomenon such as "source appearing in the output." Before entering branch A, you must at least be able to determine whether the report says that the endpoint is absent, or that the endpoint is present but the reader believes the source it refers to is wrong. If the report only says "the mapping is wrong," do not fill in the relationships among line, column, source, or end on the report's behalf. These terms may appear in the mapping materials, but they are not facts about the incident that can be inferred from the title alone.

Likewise, container adoption and JSON raws are not the default attribution when a text differs in spaces, quotation marks, or line breaks. The issue name itself puts the container and raws together, while old records also place it on the same page as map generator, which easily creates a third layer of confusion: when serialized text differs, people go looking for the map; when they see a map, they treat the container as having already been accepted. Here, samples should first be documented by processing round, rather than by the implementation name you suspect.

The minimum number of time points that must be distinguished is only three: the original input, the first result, and the second result. Not every report has a second result. When there is no second result, leave it blank; do not use an approximately matching text edited by hand to fabricate a processing run. If a second result exists, also state whether it directly uses the first result as its object or input. When editing, concatenation, or replacement occurred in between, the last two text segments cannot be placed directly into B2 even if they are similar.

An old page placed "look at map generator first" too early. That was intended to keep newcomers from having to search through the entire repository, not to suggest that the incident had already been explained by that file. Keep this entry point, but move it after the samples: only A2 should immediately look back, while B2 needs to continue tracing the relevant processing only when the source of the second-round object can already be explained. This at least prevents code reading from replacing the pairing of input, output, and map.

## A: mapped origin endpoint

### A1: no map

If the report has no map, or the remaining map cannot be matched to the same output, do not derive the endpoint from the output text. You may retain the input in its original formatting, the generated text, and the description in the report; these are clues, but they do not constitute a verifiable mapped origin endpoint. The most appropriate stopping point here is "mapping material missing."

In the past, some people routed A1 to the container branch simply because JSON raws appeared in the input. That old routing no longer applies. Text related to raws cannot restore the map, nor can it explain at which layer the endpoint disappeared. If the report separately includes a result after reprocessing, you can open a B branch; otherwise, A1 does not need to be expanded just to make the case seem complete.

A1 must not be rewritten as an ordinary unmapped source endpoint either. This page covers user-visible entry points for mapped origin endpoints; ordinary unmapped cases have a separate verification entry point, see DOC-24. Both pages can be found by searching for "source" or "endpoint", but matching search terms do not mean their samples are interchangeable.

### A2: There is a map, but the endpoint cannot be verified in the sample

A2 is where the old entry point is still useful. Put the original input, the text produced by one generation run, and the corresponding map in the same set of materials, then start at `lib/map-generator.js` and review the adjacent generation steps. Old troubleshooting records point to this file through issue names and call names; it is a suitable starting point for reading, but does not promise that every kind of missing endpoint is caused by this file alone.

You do not need to write a complete account of the calls before reading. Just record the objects and input shapes actually encountered in the current sample. If you read processing near map, source, origin, end, line, or column, first confirm whether it corresponds to the map you have on hand. Seeing the same words does not mean a relationship has been established; in particular, do not attach a map left over from another generation run to the current output.

The materials submitted for A2 can be very brief:

- An input that has not been rewritten;
- The text produced by that generation run;
- The map paired with that text;
- The endpoint that the report says cannot be verified;
- If necessary, one sentence explaining whether the map came from the same generation run.

If any of these items cannot be obtained, state what is missing rather than filling it in from memory. Old records often contain the judgment "the text looks normal, so the endpoint should be normal too"; this statement must no longer be used. Whether the text is acceptable and whether the endpoint exists are two different things.

### A3: The endpoint is visible, but the result still does not match the report

The fact that the endpoint has appeared cannot be used as a reason to rule the case out. First ask which layer the report considers "wrong": whether the source object pointed to by the endpoint is not the expected source, or whether the source object is undisputed and readers simply interpret the position differently. The former can remain in the mapping materials for further verification; for the latter, preserve how the report interprets the position, rather than just pasting terminal text and labeling it "origin is wrong".

A3 should not be merged into container adoption. Both may involve text differences, but the core of the A3 case is that the endpoint is already visible while its interpretation has not yet been agreed upon; the core of branch B is which processing pass introduced the change. If the two are merged, later readers will only see two issue names appearing together, without seeing the order in which the actual differences occurred.

The old page contains an implicit rule: "If the endpoint is visible, there is no need to keep the sample." This rule no longer applies. A visible endpoint only shows that the sample does not belong to A2; it does not explain the source or location on behalf of the report. A3 must retain at least that endpoint, the relevant map, the output, and the expected source or expected explanation stated in the report. If these are missing, you can still stop at "insufficient description"; do not fill in the user's expectations with a particular file or coordinate.

## B: container adoption and JSON raws

Samples on the container side should be as short as possible. Long style inputs draw attention to large amounts of irrelevant text; what actually needs to be examined is whether a difference appears between the first result and the next processing pass. Processing again means using the result of the first pass as the object or input of the next pass. Do not substitute another manually adjusted string for the first result, and do not retain only the final text from the second pass.

JSON raws is syntax information that needs to be retained here, not another name for a map issue. When it appears in a report, input, or output, first record which pass made it unacceptable; do not assert that container adoption has already occurred just because you see it. Conversely, having container adoption in the issue name does not mean that all changes should be attributed to the container. The old page linked these two terms into a single troubleshooting step, which is still useful for searches, but cannot serve as the current basis for attribution.

### B1: Changes already appear in the first processing pass

If the original input and the first output are already different, stop at B1 first. At this point, the most important things to retain are the location where the change first appeared and the pairing of the original input with the first output. You can include a map, but the map cannot replace the first output; nor can you reframe the case as a mapped origin endpoint merely because a map exists.

The old advice said "process it again first and see whether the issue stabilizes". This is not appropriate for B1. The first result already contains a change, so another processing pass can at most provide another piece of evidence; it cannot replace the original case. If there is indeed a second result, list it separately as supplementary material; do not let the second output overwrite the first output, or it will be impossible to determine later whether the change was already present in the first pass or grew in subsequent processing.

If B1 does not contain enough information to determine whether raws were retained, simply write "raws status unconfirmed". Do not guess based on indentation, spaces, or the shape of quotation marks. Screenshots can also be retained, but they cannot replace the input and its corresponding output.

### B2: Differences appear only in the second processing pass

B2 is the case to investigate that is closer to container adoption: the first result is still acceptable, and differences appear only after the second processing pass. The key here is not to name the phenomenon, but to make clear which object the second pass processed. Posting only two pieces of CSS that look different is not enough for someone reviewing them later to determine whether one was produced by directly processing the other.

The sequence to retain is the original input, the first output, and the second output, followed by a sentence stating where the object used in the second pass came from. If the second pass actually received manually edited intermediate text, the conditions for B2 are not met, and it should revert to B3. If the object's source was not recorded, do not write it up as a container adoption failure just because of the word "second"; at most, write "changed after repeated processing; container source still to be supplied".

The statement in old records that "container adoption is always visible only on the second pass" should be treated as deprecated shorthand. B1 already explains that differences may appear in the first pass, while B3 explains that the absence of a second pass does not mean the issue can be ruled out. A second pass is an action used to distinguish samples, not a definition, nor a step that must be artificially added for reproduction.

### B3: The sample is incomplete

When there is no second result or no container source, keep B3 and do not try to add a conclusion. The value of B3 is that it tells us what is missing for the next rerun: the original input, the first output, the second output, or the source of the object used in the second pass. Blank entries are more reliable than descriptions filled in later based on the issue name.

Materials of this kind were often changed directly to "container adoption" in old cards. Doing so makes retrieval faster, but actual regression testing harder. The issue name may remain, but the sample status should be stated clearly. As long as key materials are missing, B3 cannot be upgraded to B2 and should not be rewritten as a map branch either.

## Record format

Not every run requires a complete retrospective. The table below is the minimum layout that can be used for a regression addendum; when a field has no value, it can be left blank to avoid writing later guesses back into the state at that time.

| Observed-state field | A: mapped origin endpoint | B: container / raws |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original input | Retained | Retained |
| First output | Paired with map | Paired with the original input |
| map | If present, preserve the correspondence from the same run | May be attached; does not replace the output |
| Second output | Retain only when there was in fact another processing step | Retain for B2 |
| Report description | endpoint missing or result does not match | Changes in adoption, raws, or after repeated processing |
| Current stopping point | map missing, pairing relationship missing, or description insufficient | Second result missing, container source missing |

"Retained" in the table does not promise that every item can be fully checked. It only prevents a sample from being split across multiple places: one place containing only the input, another containing only the map, and a third containing only an impression of the final text. If map comes from another generation round, state this directly next to the sample; otherwise, it cannot be used to verify the current endpoint.

On the container side, the first and second outputs should not be mixed into the same excerpt either. For a single observed case, three clearly written lines are often enough: what the original input was, whether the first result was acceptable, and whether the second result differed. Add the object's source only when more information is needed. Do not list every possible raws form just to make it look complete.

## Old routes in the initial draft

The initial draft's routing was: when you see an origin endpoint, check the map generator first; when you see JSON raws, check the same entry point first as well. It has not been removed, because older searches and old links still bring people here. But this routing can now only serve as an order for triage, not as a basis for judging the implementation-level cause.

The working hypothesis at the time was that mapped endpoints and container acceptance might converge on the same generation path. Subsequent review did not produce enough material to state this hypothesis as a conclusion. In particular, when a container report has no second result, that absence cannot be used to prove that map generation was involved; a missing endpoint in the mapped branch also cannot automatically go into B1 just because the input contains JSON raws.

The old routing still fits two situations. First, the report includes a map and the original input, but it is not yet clear whether the endpoint is missing or its interpretation does not match; starting with `lib/map-generator.js` is safer than changing the output first. Second, the regression material already contains both the first and second results, and you need to determine which round introduced the difference; in this case, putting the two results side by side first is more effective than inferring the cause from the issue title.

The old routing does not fit two other situations: ordinary text differences without a map, and reports with only one output that are nevertheless called container adoption. The former stops at A1 or follows the entry point at DOC-24, while the latter stops at B3. Separating them leaves more unfinished items, but does not disguise gaps in the material as already classified faults.

## Card review

CSS-213 corresponds to the user-visible entry point for mapped origin endpoint. That card was later handed off and entered processing; when reviewing it, the focus is on recovering how an actual call was made and the result the user saw. If that set of material can be obtained, place it under A2 or A3; if only the issue summary remains, do not expand the summary into a reproducible sample.

CSS-230 corresponds to inconsistent observed results for container adoption and JSON raws. The note left after reviewing the documentation still points to an unconfirmed detail: the input and output are stored in a separate regression rerun log. This document does not restate that log or draw conclusions on its behalf. For the actual investigation, first obtain the shortest input and output, then place them in the appropriate branch under B1, B2, or B3.

The two cards serve different purposes. CSS-213 help reconstruct the endpoint results the user actually saw; CSS-230 help locate materials related to repeated processing. Neither can replace the samples on this page. When a card's description contradicts a sample, first check whether they came from the same processing run; if you cannot confirm this, keep the contradiction rather than choosing an issue name that sounds more plausible just to close the record.

## A few branches added after review

**The report includes a map but does not say whether the endpoint is missing.** First ask whether it is describing a source object mismatch or a mismatch in how the location is interpreted. The former can still be retained as mapping material; do not rewrite the latter as "the origin is wrong". The endpoint in the old title is not a catch-all term for every location issue.

**The report mentions both container and map.** First record the sequence of events: when the container entered processing, which output the map belongs to, and in which round the text differences appeared. If there is no sequence for these three items, record it as a mixed case. The three terms appearing together is not enough to establish that they cause one another.

**The first output has already changed.** Stay in B1 for now. You can run another processing pass as a supplement, but you cannot treat the new output as the original case. The initial draft described processing again as the default action, which could easily obscure changes that had already occurred in the first round; that recommendation no longer applies.

**The output changes only on the second pass.** Record whether the first output was used unchanged in the second round. If it was manually edited in between, the materials for B2 are insufficient, and you should return to B3. Do not draw conclusions about container acceptance when the object's source is missing.

**Only a piece of serialized text remains.** Do not infer JSON raws from indentation, spaces, or quotation marks. You can discuss whether it is preserved only when both the original input and at least one corresponding output are available. Old screenshots can serve as clues, but they cannot close the branch.

**Someone says "it has already been fixed".** First confirm whether they mean the endpoint, the container, or the text of a regression sample. These terms were used interchangeably in old records. If you cannot confirm this, retain the original statement and return to the input, output, and map that you can obtain; do not choose the closest category just to make filing easier.

## Parts of this page that can still be followed

1. Copy the original terms from the report. mapped origin endpoint, container adoption, and JSON raws may appear together, but do not immediately combine them under an umbrella term.
2. Keep the original input and the first output. If a map is available in the mapping case, keep the map together with this output; if a second output is available in the repeated-processing case, keep it separately.
3. Use the tree to determine whether the case can enter A or B. If it cannot, state the missing item directly, such as "no map" or "no second output".
4. Only in A2 should you look back from `lib/map-generator.js`; only in B2 is an explanation of the second-round object's origin required. Reversing this order lets the starting point for reading take the place of the actual case.
5. Link the shortest sample to the corresponding issue in CSS-213 or CSS-230. The link only makes it easier to refer back; it does not establish attribution.

If, by the fifth step, you still cannot answer where the endpoint is missing or in which round the difference appeared, stop. The old page used to continue tracing line, column, source, and end, often resulting in relationships absent from the report being written into the troubleshooting record. These terms are now only markers that may appear in the mapping materials; the actual sample determines whether they are relevant.

Two passages from the old notes still turn up in historical searches. They are included here so they will not be mistaken for current steps again:

> Old note: Whenever an origin endpoint error occurs, find the cause in the map generator.

This statement ignores reports without a map, as well as cases where the endpoint is visible but the result is still considered a mismatch. Under the current tree, the case should first fall into A1, A2, or A3; only A2 requires immediately looking back at that file.

> Old note: container adoption issues can only be seen after a second processing pass.

This statement no longer applies either. B1 indicates that a difference may already exist in the first round, while B3 indicates that no judgment can be made without a second round. The second processing pass is a distinguishing action, not a definition.

A supplementary note does not need to become a lengthy conclusion. On the mapping side, it can simply say, "The original input, first output, and corresponding map are available; the endpoint cannot be verified, so retain the sample under A2". On the container side, it can simply say, "The first result is acceptable, and the second result changes; the container's origin still needs to be supplied, so provisionally classify this as B2". # NoWorkResult Parser Guard Decision Record

This page originally recorded just one narrowly scoped matter: after a legacy call failed, the troubleshooting term led people to `lib/processor.js`. The initial draft did not identify this entry point as the location responsible for the implementation, nor did it describe the NoWorkResult parser guard as a confirmed mechanism. People later continued to find this page through that term, so the original assessment was not deleted; it explains why the compatibility change was not applied directly to the file found during troubleshooting at the time.

The initial draft now seems somewhat conservative in tone, but it was not without a conclusion. At the time, two approaches were genuinely compared—"change it first" and "confirm the relationship first"—and the latter was chosen. This passage is retained not to elevate the old investigation into the latest explanation, but to let later readers know that an easy approach was once rejected here because it would have treated a file path as a boundary of responsibility.

## Assessments Retained from the Initial Draft

The legacy call failure was an observation, not a localization of the problem. It showed that a call on a legacy path did not produce the result expected at the time; it did not show how far the parser had executed, nor whether the processor was responsible for the guard. The term NoWorkResult appeared in the issue name, which was enough to serve as a search clue, but not enough to combine the apparent result, the input boundary, and the file location into a single conclusion.

`lib/processor.js` was of the same nature. The match found in the old investigation narrowed the next inspection to a fixed entry point, which was its most practical role on this page. The initial draft did not preserve the complete call chain, nor did it retain any snippet that could clearly attribute the guard to the parser or processor. The path therefore cannot support any stronger meaning than "continue inspecting from here."

There was an intuition at the time: since the call name was close to the processor, first treat differences within the compatibility window as a local problem there. That intuition was not incorporated into the decision. If it was wrong, the change would introduce two unverified premises at once: that the failure had already been localized, and that the relationship between the parser and no-work results was determined only near that file. The initial draft considered both premises premature.

The other approach was to treat the file as an entry point first, then confirm what happened as references passed through it. This approach did not promise to find a particular line containing the guard, nor did it promise that the legacy call failure would necessarily become an item to fix. It only established the inspection order: first identify the objects handled by the parser, the objects received by the processor, and the circumstances that ultimately appeared as no-work results; do not designate a location for changes while the relationship remains unresolved.

The initial draft adopted the second approach. The cost was that there was no deliverable compatibility conclusion at the time, and no assessment stating "passed." The benefit was small but clear: the next round of troubleshooting would not first have to undo the assumption that "a file match identifies the implementation's responsible location."

## Interpretations Not Adopted at the Time

Treating the failed call itself as evidence that the guard had taken effect was one of the easiest ways to misread the situation. The failure could have occurred before entering the parser, at the stage where the processor received the input, or simply because the legacy path represented no-work results differently. The existing record did not rank these possibilities, so a single failure could not replace confirmation of the relationship.

Conversely, directly treating no-work results as an error return was also insufficient. No-work results are a term for the objects that this record must retain, but the old material did not map them individually to the parser's inputs, nor did it explain whether the processor was merely a pass-through point. The initial draft did not describe them as a normal branch or an error branch; both labels went beyond what was known at the time.

Another, faster way to write this up would have been to substitute the issue name for the decision itself: treat "NoWorkResult parser guard" as existing local logic with a clearly defined location, then add a compatibility explanation. That would look complete, but it would erase the most important gap. The issue name reliably points to the old investigation; it does not reliably establish the guard's location, its trigger conditions, or how the result was formed.

The initial draft therefore deliberately placed several terms side by side without merging them. The parser is a processing stage that needs confirmation; the processor is the file vicinity reached by the old record; no-work results are the result objects that appeared in the discussion. Their appearance together makes it easier to find the issue from that time; they are not the same point of responsibility.

## Diagram of the Decision's Scope

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldCallFailure
    OldCallFailure: Legacy call failure
    FileEntry: File entry point
    RelationOpen: Relationship unconfirmed
    ReferenceCheck: Recheck references
    OldCallFailure --> FileEntry: Issue name and call name
    FileEntry --> RelationOpen: Do not change directly
    RelationOpen --> ReferenceCheck: Continue inspecting
    ReferenceCheck --> RelationOpen: One point remains unconfirmed
```

"Relationship unconfirmed" in the diagram is not a newly added failure state, but the stopping point preserved by this decision. The initial draft's conclusion was never "the guard is not in the processor," nor was it "the parser has no guard." It rejected only one inference: opening `lib/processor.js` during the old investigation was not enough to directly designate the change location for the NoWorkResult parser guard.

This boundary also limits the applicability of the old decision. It addresses only the legacy call failure referred to by this issue name, does not cover other callers, does not classify all no-work results as the same compatibility issue, and makes no judgment about source map behavior. Related topics may share the term no-work, but they cannot fill in each other's call relationships that have not yet been established.

## Addendum After Review

An interface review later took place in CSS-216. The correction left after the review did not make the conclusion more definite; instead, it explicitly stated that in the Processor and no-work results section, one point about the NoWorkResult parser guard remained unconfirmed. This addendum changed how this page should be read.

The initial draft said "first continue inspecting along the references," which reads like a troubleshooting sequence yet to be completed. After the addendum, it should be read as "inspection along the references is still required." The difference is not that the approach is being proposed again, but that the interface review did not automatically turn this local relationship into a confirmed fact. The fact that a review took place only shows that the inspection passed through this area; it cannot substitute for the inspection results.

Both the old decision and the later correction are retained here. If only the initial draft remained, readers might mistakenly think the deferral was merely due to a lack of time then; if only the correction remained, readers would not see the reason for the deferral. Keeping both passages is the only way to show that the file entry point was always there, the justification for changing things directly at that entry point was always insufficient, and the later review did not eliminate that insufficiency.

The review did not leave a guard location, a complete call path, or a compatibility result. This page does not use it to supply an implementation conclusion. Nor does it expand "one point remains unconfirmed" into a claim that the entire processor or all no-work results are unreliable; the uncertainty applies only to the local relationship already delineated in this record.

## Working Tree and Cache Locations

CSS-216 also retained a specific inspection action: inspect the working tree and cache locations once before and once after executing NoWorkResult parser guard, to confirm exactly what the command changed. This action is worth retaining alongside the decision because it addresses whether the workspace changed after the legacy call failed.

However, before-and-after inspection is not equivalent to confirming references. Even if the working tree or cache locations changed, it would still be necessary to determine whether the change was caused by that operation; even if there was no change, that would only mean this inspection found no change. Neither result alone can place the guard in the parser or processor.

The initial draft did not preserve the before-and-after states or provide differences in the cache locations, so no result is added here. Writing an item awaiting inspection as completed verification would make the action on the card look like a successful reproduction; the existing record does not support that wording.

This and the file entry point are two adjacent but distinct lines of inquiry. `lib/processor.js` is used to continue identifying the local reference relationship; the working tree and cache locations are used to identify what happened in the workspace after the relevant operation was executed. The latter cannot replace the former, nor should the latter be used to prove where responsibility for the implementation lies.

## The Trade-off Still Retained

The decision retained on this page is: when faced with the legacy call failure, do not directly schedule a change to the NoWorkResult parser guard based on the file match for `lib/processor.js`. This sentence is the core of the old decision, and its scope is limited to the troubleshooting relationships preserved here.

It does not deny the processor's responsibility. The processor remains in the record precisely because the old investigation reached the relevant entry point; but the reference relationship still lies between reaching an entry point and confirming responsibility. Nor does it affirm or deny anything about the parser. The parser remains in the issue name to prevent later readers from mistaking the filename for the only boundary.

Likewise, not making a direct change for now is not a permanent prohibition. It was a choice of sequence made at the time in the face of an incomplete relationship: first reduce incorrect attribution, then discuss whether a compatibility change actually exists. The correction after the review neither elevated that choice into a stronger implementation assessment nor overturned it.

If someone later confirms the guard's location, that should produce new material specifically explaining that relationship. This page should not be retroactively rewritten as the latest statement of responsibility. The value of the old decision lies in preserving the reason for not acting on the filename at the time, not in reserving a place for a future implementation conclusion.

DOC-27 concerns an interface review of no-work source-map parity. The two pages can link to each other, but that topic cannot answer the unconfirmed point on this page about the parser guard's location; this page also does not use it to assess source map behavior. CSS-216, meanwhile, retains the legacy call failure, the interface review, and the action of inspecting the working tree and cache locations before and after execution, which is enough to explain why this page has an addendum but has still not become a completion report.

This record is still referenced because the issue name, file entry point, and reason for deferral can still help people avoid the same incorrect attribution. It is no longer a complete account of how the issue was handled. The next time `lib/processor.js` is opened from `v_prev` in `internal/postcss-core`, first record the actual reference relationship; if what is visible is still only the entry point, leave the conclusion at the entry point.

# Postmortem: User-Facing Site Dual-State Anomaly

The site's user entry point is formed jointly by docs and guide. Version notes, handling of expired content, and exit criteria are all read from here. The anomaly was not that the page could not be opened, but that the same object returned different current revisions at two observation times; the original record and recovery page therefore could not be explained under the same version note.

The sequence at the time was recorded as follows:

- The entry point was compared with the old record for the first time, and its displayed current revision was found to differ from the old record.
- When the entry point was opened again, the page showed another current revision; neither reading left enough accompanying information to explain why it had changed.
- Further retries did not converge the two readings on a single confirmable value, so the export from that time was retained and repeated checking stopped.
- The recovery page could be retrieved again, but that only showed that the material was still recoverable; it did not explain why the revision had changed.

The handling approach at the time was to treat this as a transient overwrite during an entry-page update: use the page's final displayed value, without recording the change time separately. This judgment was left in the record afterward because it made the version note appear stable, but it did not actually explain the discrepancy between the old record and the two entry readings.

The main impact was on decisions made when using the site. After entering from docs, a reader might handle expired content according to one version of the guidance; when checking back from guide, they would see a different current revision. The exit action and maintenance scope therefore cannot rely only on the value shown by the page the last time. Actions already completed under the old approach were not redone; only the record that they had occurred was retained.

The saved materials are at `docs/adj-license/incidents/LICENSE-user-documentation-portal-two-states-for-one-object.md`. They include the original record and the recovery page; the two should be viewed together, and the recovery page must not be treated as a substitute for the first reading.

What remains unconfirmed is what caused the revision to change and whether an unrecorded entry-point switch occurred between the two readings.
